items.definition: The capacity factor of a solar facility measures actual annual output against the theoretical maximum if the DC nameplate rating ran continuously.
items.core_idea: Solar plants typically realize only 10-20% of DC nameplate capacity over a year, mainly because the sun is unavailable roughly half of each day plus additional system losses; sustained output above 35% would be atypical.
key_points: Typical annual capacity factor for DC-nameplate-rated solar is 10-20%.
Location and panel technology both drive variation in realized capacity factor.
Night-time hours (roughly half the day) plus system losses cap realistic capacity factors well below 100%.
A capacity factor above 35% would be considered very unusual for solar.
relationships: Capacity factor comparisons are commonly benchmarked against wind and thermal generation, though this passage covers solar only.
trading_implications: Low and variable capacity factors mean solar output forecasts must account for seasonal/monthly patterns, not just nameplate capacity, when valuing generation or structuring supply contracts.
common_misunderstandings: Nameplate (DC) capacity significantly overstates expected average output; assuming near-nameplate generation would badly mis-forecast supply.

items.topic: Capacity factor by solar tracking technology
items.definition: Different solar panel mounting technologies (fixed, single-axis tracking, dual-axis tracking) achieve different ranges of capacity factor by more closely following the sun's position.
items.core_idea: Adding tracking motion to solar panels increases efficiency and capacity factor relative to a fixed panel, with dual-axis tracking outperforming single-axis, which in turn outperforms fixed installations.
key_points: One-axis (east-west) tracking: 25-30% more efficient than fixed panels, with 17-25% capacity factor.
Two-axis tracking (east-west plus tilt): 30-40% more efficient than fixed panels, with 18-27.5% capacity factor.
Efficiency gains from tracking come from keeping panels more directly oriented toward the sun as it moves through the sky.
relationships: Directly extends the general solar capacity factor range described alongside it.
trading_implications: Knowing which tracking technology underlies a given solar asset helps refine generation forecasts and valuation versus using a single blended capacity-factor assumption.
common_misunderstandings: The percentage efficiency gains (25-30%, 30-40%) describe relative improvement in output versus a fixed panel, not the absolute capacity factor itself.
related_topics: Cost vs. production trade-off in solar installation

items.topic: Cost vs. production trade-off in solar tracking systems
items.definition: A design trade-off exists between the simplicity/low cost of fixed solar panels and the higher output but greater expense of motorized tracking panels.
items.core_idea: Fixed panels have fewer moving parts and lower maintenance costs, while motorized tracking panels boost energy capture at the price of higher installation and maintenance costs.
key_points: Fixed installations minimize moving parts and maintenance burden.
Motorized tracking components raise both installation and ongoing maintenance costs.
The choice between fixed and tracking designs is fundamentally an economic trade-off between extra production and extra cost.
relationships: Underlies the capacity factor differences described for fixed vs. one-axis vs. two-axis tracking panels.
trading_implications: Asset-level economics (capex/opex vs. incremental generation revenue) should factor into evaluating or financing solar projects with different tracking technologies.
related_topics: Capacity factor by solar tracking technology

items.topic: German feed-in tariff solar subsidy trade
items.definition: A worked example of how a government feed-in tariff and net-metering policy created a strong financial incentive for German homeowners to install solar capacity beyond their own consumption needs.
items.core_idea: By paying homeowners roughly triple the retail power price for solar electricity exported to the grid (funded by a surcharge spread across all ratepayers), the German policy made maximizing exportable solar capacity, not just offsetting home use, the economically optimal strategy.
key_points: Feed-in tariffs paid homeowners an above-retail price for solar power fed back into the grid.
Net-metering let households simultaneously draw from and export to the grid.
The above-market cost of the subsidy was socialized monthly across all utility customers as a surcharge.
Illustrative pricing: retail power at $30/MWh vs. a feed-in payment of about $90/MWh (roughly triple).
Before a household becomes a net exporter, solar power's value is capped at the avoided cost of grid electricity; only exported surplus captures the tripled price.
Optimal homeowner strategy: install as much solar capacity as feasible and minimize home consumption to maximize the exported (grid-bound) surplus.
Once a home crosses into net-exporter status during daylight hours, the investment pays back relatively quickly given the tripled export price.
Outcome: Germany built the world's largest installed PV base despite modest solar resource; non-adopters saw only a modest utility cost increase, and solar came to cover a large share of peak demand.
relationships: Illustrates a policy-driven trading/investment incentive layered on top of the physical solar generation characteristics described earlier in the section.
trading_implications: Subsidy design (a large spread between retail and feed-in price) can make oversizing generation capacity, rather than simply matching load, the economically rational strategy.
Socialized surcharge funding means the economics of the trade depend on policy durability and the size of the non-adopter customer base absorbing the cost.
common_misunderstandings: The value of self-generated solar is not constant: it equals avoided retail cost up to self-consumption, then jumps to the (much higher) feed-in tariff rate only for exported surplus.
items.author_states_vs_inference: The author describes this explicitly as a simplified example; all figures and mechanics stated are from source, with the author's own framing that it is presented as an easy/clear-cut trade.
